  • The ratings were affirmed, with CreditWatch marking a review for a possible downgrade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, S&P Global Ratings placed NVIDIA’s AA issuer credit rating and AA senior unsecured debt rating on CreditWatch with negative implications on November 25, 2026, citing concerns about board independence, executive oversight and succession planning. The agency said it could downgrade NVIDIA within 90 days if further due diligence finds that governance deficiencies remain.

The ratings were affirmed, with CreditWatch marking a review for a possible downgrade. The issuer rating moved from AA/Stable/A-1+ to AA/Watch Neg/A-1+, while the senior unsecured rating moved from AA to AA/Watch Neg. NVIDIA’s A-1+ commercial paper rating was affirmed separately.

In a recent development, the concerns center on the board’s structure, composition and effectiveness. S&P said events involving the CEO and questions about potential export-control violations exposed those weaknesses; the CEO’s departure and later reinstatement did not resolve its questions about oversight of the executive code of conduct. Weak executive oversight and a lack of succession planning also sharpened key-person concerns.

In S&P’s assessment, long director tenures may have compromised independence, while governance practices may have lagged NVIDIA’s rapid expansion and growing importance in global technology infrastructure. The agency revised the management-and-governance modifier used in its credit analysis to neutral from positive and was unaware of any remedial board action addressing the potential deficiencies.

Industry observers note that S&P intends to meet NVIDIA’s board and management to discuss board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession proposal. It expects any downgrade to be limited to one notch unless investigations or disclosures indicate harm to NVIDIA’s reputation or future business prospects.

In a recent development, export controls form a separate part of the assessment. NVIDIA’s China exposure raises questions about geopolitical risk management and internal controls, in S&P’s view. A conclusion that export-control rules were circumvented or violated, or that past disclosures about exposure to China and nearby regions were misleading or understated, would weigh on overall credit quality.

In a recent development, for now, S&P’s assessments of NVIDIA’s competitive position, technology leadership and financial profile remain unchanged. S&P said stricter export controls could reduce future growth prospects, while its published scores still classify business risk as strong, competitive position as excellent, financial risk as minimal and liquidity as exceptional, with an aa stand-alone credit profile.

The credit profile rests on a business S&P describes as data-center-scale AI infrastructure. Its platform covers chips, networking, systems and software for model training and inference, data analytics, scientific computing, robotics and 3D graphics. Compute and networking generated 90% of revenue in the fiscal year ended January 25, 2026, while graphics generated 10%. Its core end markets are data center, gaming, professional visualization and automotive.

According to recent reports, the review therefore separates NVIDIA’s operating and financial strength from the governance controls around it. S&P is testing whether board oversight and succession planning have kept pace with the company’s role in AI infrastructure; adverse export-control or disclosure findings could broaden the concern to its reputation and business prospects.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

According to recent reports, to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Sources indicate that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Sources indicate that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Sources indicate that here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below rolls out training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Sources indicate that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Recent findings suggest that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

In a recent development, make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, customers can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.

The Australian uranium producer stated on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.

Peninsula Energy mentioned it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected.

"The organization's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it noted in an enhancement to the Australian Securities Exchange.

The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing.

According to recent reports, peninsula has not given a restart date and states it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said.

The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site.

The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time.

Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance.

Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈.

Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors.

The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb.

Recent findings suggest that peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®.

FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Recent findings suggest that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the substantial matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Recent findings suggest that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Sources indicate that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In a recent development, in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Sources indicate that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

It has been revealed that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

According to recent reports, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Recent findings suggest that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Recent findings suggest that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Sources indicate that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

It has been revealed that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Industry observers note that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Sources indicate that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

In a recent development, bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Sources indicate that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.
  • Sources indicate that in a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz stated its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers face frantic scramble to migrate workloads and rotate compromised credentials.

Rackspace is shutting down its low-cost Spot cloud service after a security breach, giving customers two weeks' notice to move their workloads and retrieve their data.

Sources indicate that in a notice posted on Tuesday, the cloud computing biz stated its Rackspace Spot service will cease operations at 1700 Central Time (2300 UTC) on December 8. Any workloads still running at that point will be terminated, and customers will no longer be able to access their data.

"Following the recent security incident affecting Rackspace Spot, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the service," the company stated. "Spot customers are being notified with the wind-down timeline, instructions for retrieving their data and steps to secure their environments.".

Customers will have to contend with the fallout from the breach while simultaneously trying to get their applications and data off the platform.

According to a customer notification seen by The Register, the attackers used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot over a period of almost 22 hours on November 17. Rackspace only learned of the intrusion the following day, after a customer raised the alarm.

The intruders impersonated legitimate users, created pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, gained access to stored credentials known as Kubernetes Secrets, and listed nodes and storage volumes.

"With that access, they could have read any Secret in an affected user's clusters, and any Spot API token or refresh token that user held," Rackspace told customers.

Rackspace has since revoked the affected tokens and sessions, removed the pods planted by the intruders, and changed the affected platform and storage keys. Customers must also reissue API tokens, download new Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their clusters, including database passwords and third-party API keys.

Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and chief growth officer of Platform9, which co-developed Spot with Rackspace, shed some light on the root cause in a November 20 GitHub post.

In a recent development, "An observability system was breached using a compromised credential," Raghuram wrote. "This was obviously a critical error on our part and we are very sorry we let this happen.".

Raghuram remarked the incident necessitated significant changes to the underlying infrastructure clusters, prolonging the outage.

Spot's selling point was cheap compute. The service operated an auction-based pricing model, allowing customers to bid for cloud infrastructure at a fraction of the cost of conventional on-demand instances. Rackspace advertised savings of up to 90 percent for customers willing to tolerate interruptions to their workloads. A permanent interruption probably wasn't what they had in mind.

According to recent reports, rackspace hasn't explained why it chose closure over recovery, revealed how many customers were affected, or said whether it will offer migration extensions. It did not respond to The Register's questions. ®.

Browser tabs as a container runtime

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fzakaria

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tl;dr tabc is a container runtime, like runc, that runs each container in a Chromium tab.
  • In a recent development, despite my zealot love for Nix, there is no denying the convenience and ubiquity of Docker.
  • Despite all the footguns you can get yourself into by writing a non-reproducible Dockerfile, it was a still a remarkable step forward in making software deployment more predictable and portable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tl;dr tabc is a container runtime, like runc, that runs each container in a Chromium tab. docker run --runtime tabc alpine works and starts in under a second. On a Mac it needs no hypervisor and no Linux VM; Linux for everyone!

In a recent development, despite my zealot love for Nix, there is no denying the convenience and ubiquity of Docker. Containers have become the standard unit of software deployment, providing a consistent environment across different machines and simplifying the management of dependencies.11Containers are not even a “real” thing within the Linux kernel although there are recent attempts to formalize them as a kernel-level abstraction.

Despite all the footguns you can get yourself into by writing a non-reproducible Dockerfile, it was a still a remarkable step forward in making software deployment more predictable and portable.

According to recent reports, nothing has really challenged Docker’s dominance in the container space and it’s reliance on Linux as the underlying platform. The absurdity of the situation has become that developers on MacOS end up running a Linux virtual machine to simply run containers.

People, even the creator of Docker, believed a common runtime for software isolation would have been a game-changer and that WebAssembly could have played that role if it had existed earlier.

Recent findings suggest that “If WASM+WASI existed in 2008, we wouldn’t have needed to created Docker. That’s how notable it is.” - Solomon Hykes, 2019.

Here we are, 7 years later, we still have Docker, and WebAssembly is mostly used for speeding up web applications.

Is there another way to achieve the same level of isolation and portability without relying on the host being Linux?

What if though Docker ran its containers on WebAssembly instead of directly on the Linux kernel?

What if the isolation provided by the browser could replace the kernel-level isolation that containers rely on?

According to recent reports, this idea, the holy grail of running Linux in a browser is not upcoming. JSLinux did it in 2011, and v86, WebVM and qemu-wasm are also attempts in the same direction. They all have their share of limitations: 32-bit only, performance concerns, incomplete hardware emulation, that make them impractical for general-purpose use.

unkernel is a newly developed project by Pooya Parsa that changes the economics of what is possible. unknernel compiles the Linux kernel to WebAssembly, allowing it to run directly in the browser without relying on traditional hardware emulation. Only your container’s own code goes through an emulator, and everything else the kernel does runs at near native speed.

It is now practical to run Linux containers directly in the browser, leveraging the isolation provided by WebAssembly and the browser environment with acceptable performance.

That is a real docker run, on a real Docker daemon, starting a real Alpine image. This works even on a Mac with no Docker installed and no Linux virtual machine running. 🤯.

In my last post I was inspired from Gary Bernhardt’s The Birth & Death of JavaScript and its discussion of the evolution of software isolation.

In the talk, Bernhardt imagines a project called METAL that moves the JavaScript VM into the kernel. The VM already keeps programs apart, so the hardware no longer has to. Process isolation becomes the VM’s job.

According to recent reports, we did not need to move the VM into the kernel. A browser tab is the VM Bernhardt imagined.

Industry observers note that tabc is a OCI container runtime that runs each container in its own browser tab. That means you can use it with Docker just like any other runtime.

Whereas the default Docker runtime, runc, starts your program as a process on the host’s kernel, tabc leverages the browser as its execution environment, running each container in a separate tab with its own instance of the Linux kernel compiled to WebAssembly.22The tab boots unkernel, and the “container” runs within it.

It has been revealed that this is the part that I’m most excited about: at no point does your container ever touch the host’s kernel and require Linux. All tabc asks of the host is a browser, nothing needs Linux underneath.

In a recent development, this is a complete rethinking of the container stack on macOS. Docker on a Mac is a Linux virtual machine with a nice installer. Docker Desktop, Colima, OrbStack and Podman Machine all boot a Linux VM first. Even Apple’s own container tool boots a VM per container.

Isn’t WebAssembly a virtual machine? Technically yes, in the same way the JVM is: it runs code for a made-up CPU. The difference is that it is all software. Nothing asks macOS for a hypervisor.

It has been revealed that on Linux, Docker pulls the image and hands it to tabc. A Mac with no Linux VM has no Docker daemon to do that, so tabc run pulls the image itself.

Without Linux and namespaces, what is giving the container its isolation?

Browsers such as Chromium are an incredibly battle-tested sandbox, and we only use them for web pages. 🤦 Rather than simply relying on the host kernel’s isolation mechanisms, tabc leverages the browser’s sandbox to create an additional layer of security.33Every container may also get a browser of its own, with its own profile, so two containers share no process and no storage.

Starting a container in a browser tab is surprisingly fast, and most of the time is spent starting the browser itself. On my Linux laptop44I ran fifteen runs of echo hi from an Alpine bundle on a Ryzen 7 7840U. a container takes roughly 0.87 seconds from command to exit. This startup cost can be eliminated by using your browser’s already running instance via --open or --link, more on that later.

Unkernel has drastically improved the performance of running Linux in the browser but since the processes themselves are still emulated, there can be some noticeable delay for larger compute-heavy workloads.

According to recent reports, aside You can get a sense of the performance impact on a lot of packages by visiting https://trynix.dev. You have access to over 300,000 packages from Nixpkgs that run directly in your browser using Unkernel.

Although some of these slowdowns seem excessive, many workloads are still well within acceptable limits for interactive use that let this go beyond trivial examples and novelty.

Depending on whether you have every container running in its own browser instance or sharing tabs within a single browser, the memory overhead can be more dramatic. An idle container costs ~540 MiB of host memory split between the tab that holds the guest, the browser process, and helper processes.55For scale, Firecracker quotes under 5 MiB of overhead per microVM and 125 ms to boot.

Nevertheless, this overhead is acceptable for many interactive use cases where the convenience of running containers in browser tabs outweighs the memory cost.

Did you remember when I said you can run this on MacOS without a Linux VM !?

Video: the trading floor in The Wolf of Wall Street. Matthew McConaughey's character stands up and shouts "holy fucking shit".

Aside The idea of a container in WebAssembly was attempted before with container2wasm. It however emulated the entire machine, including the kernel, rather than just the program so it was way heavier and slower than what tabc does.

By default the browser is hidden. It does not have to be. Ready to cook ? 🧑‍🍳.

This is where the idea kind of comes together and becomes borderline magical: the browser tab itself becomes the container, and you can interact with it just like any other tab.

According to recent reports, with --open, tabc leverages the desktop environment to open the container’s page in the default browser. Even crazier is that the page itself is a pty, so you have cross-terminal interaction between the browser tab and the terminal you started it from.

Industry observers note that video: a terminal at the top runs tabc with --open, and a tab in the Chromium window under it boots Linux and highlights a shell prompt. A command typed into the tab appears in the terminal, and one typed into the terminal appears in the tab. nginx is started in the container, and a second tab at localhost:8123 shows the page it serves.

You then can visit the container’s web server at the port exposed, in this case localhost:8123, in you guessed it: another browser tab in the same browser.

Sources indicate that once you have containers you can start, they then can become composed: docker compose. Nothing beyond the runtime: tabc key in the Compose file changes. Everything else from compose continues to work: network, volumes, and all.66The --dashboard flag opens the tabc dashboard, where the tabs are panes in a single browser page.

Tip Since MacOS has no Docker daemon for compose, tabc brings its own lightweight one to handle it: tocker.

We just started two containers in the browser: a web server and a Redis instance, each running in its own tab pane and communicating with each other by service name.

Unix’s substantial bet was that everything is a file. In the browser, everything is a tab. Our mail, our editors and our terminals already moved there. We can now add containers to the list.

Industry observers note that that works on Linux and on an Apple Silicon Mac on any recent browser.77On Linux the Nix package brings its own Chromium unless you pass --open. The README has more details on setup and usage.

Recent findings suggest that solomon Hykes was half right. WebAssembly became the runtime, and Docker stayed anyway.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Recent findings suggest that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

In a recent development, the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Industry observers note that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too substantial to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Sources indicate that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the fresh provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

In a recent development, community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Industry observers note that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've slowly been moving my servers from Ubuntu 22 and 24 to 26 this year, and noticed my Ansible automation starts failing if I have password protection for sudo use:.
  • Apparently Ubuntu's been rewriting system utilities in Rust, and the sudo-rs version that ships on Ubuntu 26.04 has some incompatiblities with the sudo I've used on servers for 20+ years.
  • It prints an extra string before the password prompt, which sudo doesn't do, and that can confuse automation tools like Ansible that wait for a specific prompt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've slowly been moving my servers from Ubuntu 22 and 24 to 26 this year, and noticed my Ansible automation starts failing if I have password protection for sudo use:.

Apparently Ubuntu's been rewriting system utilities in Rust, and the sudo-rs version that ships on Ubuntu 26.04 has some incompatiblities with the sudo I've used on servers for 20+ years.

It prints an extra string before the password prompt, which sudo doesn't do, and that can confuse automation tools like Ansible that wait for a specific prompt.

There's a thread in the Ansible project covering the concern: validate sudo become plugin against sudo-rs . The fix landed in Ansible Core 2.22.0, and is being backported into updates in 2.16, 2.18, 2.19, 2.20, and maybe also 2.21 (it's quite disruptive!). It looks like it also broke pyinfra, and their fix is in the latest release of 3.11.

I updated Ansible (pip install -U ansible) and now -K (--ask-become-pass) works again.

Another alternative is to use the traditional version of sudo that still ships with Ubuntu 26. For that, the easiest way is to set the become_exe inside your hosts file:.

Or you could even revert sudo systemwide on your Ubuntu host:.

Sources indicate that I'm not sure why Ubuntu sees the need to rewrite common Linux utils in Rust. I don't mind Rust, but these are foundational tools every Linux system relies on. This isn't a window manager, where experimentation is more acceptable1.

If other distros plan on moving to sudo-rs that's one thing, but if it's just Ubuntu, maybe I should hop back to Debian for everything, and not just my cloud servers.

In a recent development, yes, I know this makes me sound like "old man yells at [rust]," but major changes to structural components of Linux should take longer, IMO. At least on the Red Hat side, we have Fedora, which is more bleeding edge, then at least a few years' gap before it hits 'production' systems. With Ubuntu, there is no cutting edge upstream where things like this can be fixed or worked around before hitting prod! (And no, I don't consider non-LTS Ubuntu releases the same thing.) ↩︎.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The latest attack in spate of similar incidents targeting booking systems globally.
  • Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) states "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.
  • The Brisbane-headquartered organization noted the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The latest attack in spate of similar incidents targeting booking systems globally.

Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) states "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack.

The Brisbane-headquartered organization noted the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents.

Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated.

Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident.

Sources indicate that an initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information.

Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the firm said.

Sources indicate that "FLT values customer privacy and data security," the organization noted in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes.".

Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said.

The organization mentioned it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their plans.

Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information.

The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels.

More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October.

Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time.

Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated.

Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft.

Sources indicate that speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or quickly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach.

"Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®.

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • Recent findings suggest that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Recent findings suggest that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Sources indicate that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

According to recent reports, the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Industry observers note that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

It has been revealed that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Sources indicate that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Recent findings suggest that decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

According to recent reports, we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Sources indicate that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

According to recent reports, it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel looks. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an matter and tell us about it.

Make the Plan a Value

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jackkelly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client token support provided by AWS.
  • Recent findings suggest that to untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, âmake the initiative a valueâ or âdecide what to do, and then do itâ.
  • I really like this pattern because the âdeciding what to doâ part of a program is often more complicated than the âdoingâ part.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client token support provided by AWS. Implementing this required making some fairly substantial changes to the generator, the bespoke Haskell program that turns the service definitions in botocore into cabal packages. amazonka is over a decade old, and the generator has evolved as AWS have added latest styles of APIs for their different services. Some services return XML, some return JSON, some return raw bytes, some return additional information in HTTP response headers, and so on. As a result, the generatorâs logic had been extended each time and had grown gnarly.

Recent findings suggest that to untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, âmake the initiative a valueâ or âdecide what to do, and then do itâ. This move decouples two parts of a program by introducing an intermediate data structure (a âplanâ, or a value of a âplan typeâ) describing what is to be done before any action is taken.

I really like this pattern because the âdeciding what to doâ part of a program is often more complicated than the âdoingâ part. Separating the two often turns the âdecidingâ part into a pure function that produces a strategy, making test cases simpler to write. And then if the âdoingâ phase is also complicated (because of remote API calls, rollbacks, parallel execution, or whatever else), itâs more manageable because those complications are not entangled with the planning logic. You also get to add a --dry-run flag almost for free, which is really useful for testing. (Henrik observes that testing for a dryRun variable everywhere pollutes the code somewhat. I think if he split his code into a planning phase and consumed that plan with either a âdry runâ printer or a ârealâ executor, the inline checks that he dislikes would disappear.).

Sources indicate that this technique isnât subtle or obscure. Iâve seen it called the plan-execute pattern, and the ârouting slipâ enterprise integration pattern is literally about centralising the decision logic before execution. Iâve previously called it a âtiny DSLâ, and Matt Parsons sells its benefits in his Three Layer Haskell Cake article:.

Having resolved to introduce a initiative type, how do we work it into a venerable program like the Amazonka generator? For this part of the generator, it means separating the analysis of the loaded service definitions from the generation of the instance AWSRequest declarations. I did this by introducing a Config record of simple data and a function instanceD :: Config -> Decl () that builds Haskell code from that config record.

Sources indicate that I found the generatorâs logic too difficult to understand and replace in a single change, so I replaced it incrementally using the strangler fig pattern. The most complicated part of this change was response parsing, so I added to the Config record an enumeration of ported response parsers, and a fall back to âdo things the old wayâ for everything else:.

It has been revealed that one thing that makes Amazonkaâs generator rewarding to hack on is that the service bindings act as an extensive and automatic golden test suite. Any changes to the generated bindings show up in diffs, and so if there are no diffs and the generator doesnât crash, the change probably didnât break anything. This makes the process of replacing the entangled code relatively simple (not easy):.

Recent findings suggest that the end result worked well and kept the individual commits readable (example: factoring out status code parsing). Adding the idempotency machinery was then straightforward.

The data types in the Amazonka example represent parameters to a Haskell code template, but this refactoring also works for more expressive plan types, such as âtiny DSLsâ, âlists of commandsâ, or âfree structuresâ. The trick is to keep a âdo it the old wayâ constructor in your plan type until the âold wayâ has been refactored away.

A well-chosen blueprint type introduces a narrow waist that decouples producers and consumers of your plan type, and the most obvious wins come from introducing alternate consumers of the plan: things like testability, --dry-run, and simpler executors all follow from that. A less obvious benefit is that you can also analyse and transform the plan itself. This is a great place to add pre-execution sanity checks or access controls. I regret that my tiny DSLs post inverted a transformation by interpreting it as matrix multiplications and inverting the result; it would have been simpler to provide an invert :: [Transform] -> [Transform] function.

Introducing alternate producers of the proposal type can also pay off, but needs a bit more imagination:.

âMaking the plan a valueâ works well in any language, but Haskellâs laziness makes it especially nice. Lazy evaluation can avoid materialising the whole plan in memory if it is consumed right away. Even in strict languages, the decoupling benefits are great enough that the extra memory use is often worth it.

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • Industry observers note that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

Industry observers note that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

According to recent reports, neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

Industry observers note that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

In a recent development, the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

It has been revealed that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table indicates which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Recent findings suggest that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

According to recent reports, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Recent findings suggest that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Industry observers note that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

According to recent reports, with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

According to recent reports, the table indicates one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Recent findings suggest that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Sources indicate that key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Sources indicate that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GeoIntelX announced on November 26, 2026, a collaboration with the Instituto Geológico de Angola and Ivanhoe Mines’ exploration team to apply artificial intelligence to more than a century of Angola’s historical geological records.

Industry observers note that ivanhoe Mines is funding the platform’s implementation in Angola, including digitization of historical geological maps, reports and other physical records held in the country’s geological archives. IGEO is the government institution responsible for managing those national archives, so the work combines a manufacturer-funded exploration tool with digitization of a public collection.

Sources indicate that ivanhoe is conducting its Angolan work through Cuando-Recursos, its wholly owned subsidiary. The copper exploration program covers more than 22,000 square kilometres in the Moxico and Cuando provinces. GeoIntelX describes the package as one of the region’s largest greenfield programs targeting sediment-hosted copper deposits.

Tim Williams, Ivanhoe Mines’ vice president of geosciences, noted the collaboration should accelerate evaluation of prospective targets, letting his team concentrate on the most promising areas and surfacing geological insights that could otherwise take years to uncover. The expected results are more efficient exploration and a better chance of discoveries, alongside local geological and technical skills development.

Sources indicate that geoIntelX notes its GIX platform digitizes and structures historical reports, georeferences geological maps and integrates the information through geospatial search. For maps and reports created separately, that location-based structure allows them to be searched as one body of evidence. The process is intended to turn physical material into accessible data for identifying and evaluating prospective mineral targets.

According to recent reports, the platform also provides chat-based access to AI agents trained for geological work, which GeoIntelX says lets geoscientists, executives and operations leads assess geological potential, economic constraints and infrastructure needs from available information. Exploration teams internationally already use the technology.

Co-founder and CEO Gilad Hoshen remarked making historical data accessible again could help exploration teams “avoid unnecessary data re-acquisition, assess opportunities faster and make better-informed decisions.”.

IGEO’s mandate includes promoting and coordinating geological research and mapping, studying Angola’s mineral resources and rocks, and managing information produced by geological and mining studies authorized in the country. The archive work therefore affects more than Ivanhoe’s workflow: it concerns how Angola preserves and accesses geological knowledge gathered by companies and institutions.

#139274. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
