How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2211 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In a recent development, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Industry observers note that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In a recent development, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Industry observers note that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

Recent findings suggest that the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

It has been revealed that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

It has been revealed that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Recent findings suggest that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Sources indicate that think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

Sources indicate that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a upcoming idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

Industry observers note that they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

Sources indicate that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Industry observers note that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

It has been revealed that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

In a recent development, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

According to recent reports, getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

According to recent reports, the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Recent findings suggest that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned.

Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation.

Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise.

According to recent reports, edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment.".

That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to.".

Recent findings suggest that the latest review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried.

It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged.

Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination.

The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review.

According to recent reports, monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs.

And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report.

The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions.

Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a newly introduced board-led governance model.

The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November.

"We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," remarked DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy.

According to recent reports, the watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cournot Protocol said in a November 26, 2026 announcement that it had raised $5 million in strategic funding co-led by Paper Ventures and Beam Foundation. The capital will fund a verifiable intelligence layer for onchain applications and AI agents.

According to recent reports, cournot’s stated mission is to expand what oracles can do beyond structured data, using AI to interpret real-world events while preserving a record that allows the resulting judgment to be checked. The funding consequently centers on verification infrastructure for automated decisions, where the path to an answer matters alongside the answer itself.

In a May 14, 2026 product description, Cournot noted its system aggregates multiple sources in real time and applies multi-agent reasoning to reach a judgment. Under that design, the sources, intermediate reasoning and final conclusion can each be proven cryptographically onchain, allowing the resulting judgment to be checked.

It has been revealed that the multi-agent component coordinates the analytical work, while the cryptographic record supplies an audit trail for the inputs and steps behind a conclusion. Cournot is addressing whether an answer can be inspected and substantiated, a separate concern from generating a fluent or plausible response. The approach also makes the reasoning process part of the oracle’s output, giving verification a defined role within the system.

In a recent development, cournot is building for BNB Chain, where it wants markets, autonomous agents and other onchain applications to use these judgments when settling against real-world outcomes. A settlement can depend on the judgment such a system produces. Building verification into that process gives the application a way to examine the evidence and reasoning attached to an outcome when deciding how to settle.

In its May 14, 2026 cohort announcement, YZi Labs listed Cournot among the EASY Residency Season 3 graduates and described the problem it was targeting: probabilistic AI answers that lack checkable reasoning, addressed by organizing intelligence into structured claims that can be audited.

YZi Labs runs EASY Residency as its main global incubator, bringing together founders working across Web3, AI and biotechnology. The cohort presentation identified markets, governance and science as high-stakes domains for Cournot’s work, where verifiable reasoning was presented as a prerequisite for placing capital and trust on AI-generated conclusions.

Sources indicate that the fresh round follows earlier backing from YZi Labs through that residency. Both the incubation thesis and the product design focus on converting probabilistic model outputs into structured claims whose evidence and reasoning can be audited. The new capital supports the development of that mechanism as infrastructure for other applications and agents.

It has been revealed that cournot’s approach changes what its oracle is expected to deliver: a judgment accompanied by an examinable basis for relying on it. For settlement and other high-stakes uses, that verifiable basis connects probabilistic AI output to the automated action Cournot intends to support.

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done.
  • In a recent development, we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

In a recent development, we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

It has been revealed that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Sources indicate that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Sources indicate that training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

Industry observers note that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but organization policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

Industry observers note that thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly latest solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In a recent development, in our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

Industry observers note that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 reveals which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

According to recent reports, table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Sources indicate that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

Sources indicate that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Sources indicate that overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

According to recent reports, pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

According to recent reports, table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

According to recent reports, figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

Sources indicate that the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

It has been revealed that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Recent findings suggest that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Sources indicate that figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

It has been revealed that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

It has been revealed that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

In a recent development, why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

According to recent reports, we used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

It has been revealed that each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

In a recent development, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

Industry observers note that we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Sources indicate that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

In a recent development, when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

Garage v2.6.0 released with web admin, v1.x EoL & other news

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deuxfleurs

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-new web administration UI funded by NLnet.
  • The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present new features and give some information on what's coming next.
  • This is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-new web administration UI funded by NLnet. We also discuss many other small news: Helm chart repository release, Garage v1.x EoL, Garage v3.0.0 beta 1 and an outlook on upcoming work on S3 versioning.

The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present new features and give some information on what's coming next.

This is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander. We started this collaboration in 2024 when it was clear that a user interface was one of the most sorely lacking feature of Garage. We are very grateful that NLnet has again engaged with us and provided funding to make this a reality.

Here's a minimal example to test 2.6.0 right away:.

Running 2.6.0 or above, you can access the web interface on the garage admin API port, by default port 3903, so http://localhost:3903/ if you are running garage on your machine with the example above.

According to recent reports, logging in requires a garage admin token. The example above prints it on the command line. If you have set the admin_token configuration variable in your configuration file, you may use that token. Otherwise, you'll need to create a separate token from the command line with garage admin-token create.

Sources indicate that one world of caution: administering a remote cluster over plain HTTP is NOT safe, as your admin token is transmitted in plain text with each request. You'll need to setup an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of your Garage node to encrypt the connection, or/and access your node through a VPN such as Wireguard to make sure no one can eavesdrop the credentials.

Once logged in the cluster, you will be greeted by a cluster overview screen that looks like the following (this is a live example from our Deuxfleurs cluster):.

Sources indicate that the web interface follows a similar pattern to the CLI: cluster monitoring, layout configuration, bucket and access credential management are all available as you expect. Here are example videos (now included in the Quick Start guide as well) showing the setting up of a new cluster from scratch:.

From a development standpoint, the web UI presently lives in a separate Git repository so please report any issues there and not in Garage's main issue tracker. Tixie will continue being the maintainer of the UI moving forward.

This has also been one of the longstanding requests from our Kubernetes consumers, and it's now done! Starting today you can deploy Garage on Kubernetes easily thanks to our self-hosted Helm repository. Both "regular" (tgz+index.yml) helm chart repository as well as OCI artefacts are available. Instructions in the documentation have been updated accordingly. Happy Helming!

Industry observers note that thanks to Boris M. and Maximilien for contributing this improvement to Garage, along the many contributors that participated in finding the right way to make this work.

The Garage helm chart follows its own version scheme, with the current version being 0.10.7.

The last release of the 1.x branch was v1.3.1 in January 2026, almost a year ago. Many significant bug fixes, including security fixes, are at the moment only present on the v2.x branch. At this point, it would be too much work to backport them to 1.x and it didn't seem there was any ask to do so from the community either. So we are officially deprecating Garage v1.x and urging all customers still on this branch to update to v2.x as soon as possible. The release note has been updated accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that we have published a first beta release of Garage v3.0.0. This release does not yet include S3 versioning (sorry!). This unfortunately needed to be a major release because of a few breaking changes we wanted to release without waiting for s3 versioning to come though:.

We are looking for testers for this beta so please give it a try and report any findings on our matter tracker!

This beta release also marks the first step toward having a reliable Fjall metadata engine so please report to us not only problems, but also cases of successfully running a Garage cluster on Fjall with significant activity, so that we can gain confidence that it works well and potentially mark it stable soon. This also means we'll take bug report for Fjall problems, something that we explicitly disregarded so far for the 2.x experimental implementation.

As per the release notes, the most crucial breaking changes for customers to be aware of are:.

To finally align with industry standard, most Prometheus metrics have been slighly renamed, we provide an updated Grafana dashboard.

Sources indicate that the Fjall major version enhancement breaks compatibility with the Garage 2.x Fjall as data files from older versions are not supported. If you were using Fjall on v2.x, you will need to migrate manually: convert your metadata to another format (LMDB or SQlite) with garage node convert-db before upgrading. You can convert back to Fjall once you successfully upgraded to v3.

The complete list of breaking changes can be found in the changelog linked above. Happy testing!

Finally we want to close this post with an update on S3 versionning.

In 2027 we will start a new collaboration with Armaël to implement what is certainly the most requested feature in Garage: S3 object versioning.

We understand that there has been growing impatience for this feature to be implemented in Garage, and rightfully so as it would enable fresh use-cases such as for long-term archiving where compliance is important, or as a backup target that cannot be tampered with.

We thank the community for their patience, and kindly ask them to understand why this hasn't been done before: while there have been several attempts by community members, this is a deep problem that requires intricate understanding of how Garage stores metadata, and implementing it without taking this into account leads to code that, while it might appear to work on the surface, is in fact incorrect. A correct implementation requires a significant rewrite of core parts of Garage, which we believe can currently be accomplished only by experienced maintainers. We will also take this rewrite as an opportunity to fix some performance problems, such as those arising with extremely big objects.

Industry observers note that I would like to make an important note on object locking and WORM: we will provide an implementation of locking primitives/WORM per the S3 API specification, however note that due to Garage's lack of a consensus algorithm, this implementation will not be fully correct. This means that Garage will implement best-effort detection of access requests that would violate locks, but will not be able to guarantee that it upholds locks in all cases. More precisely: using conditional writes (If-Match, If-None-Match) as a substitute for a distributed mutex or to discriminate between concurrent write requests will obviously not work, but ensuring that a successfully uploaded object cannot be overwritten after the fact should work in most cases. We will take care of properly documenting what works and what doesn't, but in practice, this means that locking and WORM will be gated behind a feature flag (a configuration parameter) that requires cluster administrators to acknowledge that they might be running unsafe workloads if they don't understand exactly what the feature does.

Thanks for reading, and for your continued support in our journey to a robust and resilient distributed storage system.

Alex, Maximilien and Tixie, The Garage (and Garage UI!) Maintainers.

BharatGen Releases Patram 1.5 with Promptable OCR and Abstention

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, bharatGen introduced Patram 1.5 on November 25, 2026, a 7.8-billion-parameter open-weight vision-language model for document intelligence.
  • A text-first extraction pipeline can flatten information that gives a document meaning.
  • Recent findings suggest that OCR 3.0 turns the prompt into the extraction specification.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, bharatGen introduced Patram 1.5 on November 25, 2026, a 7.8-billion-parameter open-weight vision-language model for document intelligence. Its two central additions are prompt-controlled OCR and abstention, the ability to hold back an answer when evidence is missing or conflicting, the input is unreadable, or the question is ambiguous.

A text-first extraction pipeline can flatten information that gives a document meaning. Patram instead processes page images directly, preserving visual cues such as table rows and columns, blank form fields, tick boxes, signatures, stamps and the relationships inside diagrams. Its six task areas cover document and element parsing, question answering, key-value extraction, OCR 3.0 and abstention, with inputs including handwriting, complex tables, charts and formulas.

Recent findings suggest that OCR 3.0 turns the prompt into the extraction specification. A user can select a whole page, a region or a semantic element; exclude unwanted material; retain text, structure, styling, layout or readability information; and request text, Markdown, HTML, JSON, LaTeX or Mermaid output. Field names can come from the user, structures can be flat or nested, and personal details can be masked during extraction.

Recent findings suggest that one BharatGen example asks for only the electricity-bill months above 2,000 units and returns four JSON records containing month, units and amount, rather than the entire bill. That illustrates how extraction can move filtering and formatting into the model request, reducing the separate parsing work around it.

Abstention addresses a different failure: a confident value that the page cannot support. BharatGen’s triggers include an absent answer, source material that cannot be read as requested, an ambiguous question, a false premise and conflicting evidence. The model can answer the readable portion, explain what is missing, assign confidence to individual values, request a clearer copy or identify a best guess for review.

That behavior connects to BharatGen’s workflow design, in which the model reads and extracts, code checks the details, and people handle decisions that need review. For regulated or sensitive paperwork, the practical value is a documented reason for routing doubtful values to a person while allowing clearer answers to proceed.

BharatGen evaluated Patram 1.5 on 15 PatramBench tasks and 34 public benchmarks against 27 other systems: 20 vision-language models and seven OCR or parsing systems. Every reported score came from BharatGen’s own runs under the same settings. The overall score equally weights the PatramBench and public results.

Industry observers note that on that combined measure, BharatGen reports 83; its component scores are 85 on PatramBench and 81 on the public benchmarks. Patram is level with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, listed at 403 billion and 763 billion parameters respectively. Those larger models each scored 82 on the public component, compared with Patram’s 81, so the overall parity does not mean it led every part of the evaluation.

According to recent reports, bharatGen’s token comparison uses the same 10 question-answering tests. It reports that Patram produced 21 answers in the number of tokens Qwen3.5-9B used for one thinking-mode answer, while both scored 85. The measurement covers tokens written, not inference speed, so the result concerns output efficiency and leaves comparative response speed unresolved.

It has been revealed that the published evaluation has explicit language limits. Its 15 PatramBench tasks contain 11,828 items drawn from 8,773 English document pages, while the public benchmarks use English test items only. The stated language scope is English and code-mixed pages. The full PatramBench account of its pages and 86 tasks is still forthcoming, while the AIKosh listing claims a technical report detailing limitations and failure modes will follow.

BharatGen says the model can run on a single GPU. Together with the downloadable weights, that gives organizations the option of processing sensitive documents on their own servers or cloud, keeping pages inside their own systems.

In a recent development, the vision-model page describes a limited Playground preview with 1,000 free credits per user. It includes Chat, Parse, Extract, Classify, Split and Section tools, plus ready-made workflows for identity verification, loan underwriting, health claims and contract work. API access remains on a waitlist.

Industry observers note that for researchers and document-heavy organizations, the release offers a compact model they can examine and run locally, with promptable extraction shaping the data and abstention marking the values that still need human review. That combination addresses two practical barriers to document automation: keeping sensitive pages under the user’s control and concentrating review on uncertain values instead of every field.

Breaking: OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.
  • Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.
  • In a recent development, openAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

In a recent development, openAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches.

Pando now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo and is serving nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, and each push can in turn trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history. Pando went into production in April 2026.

Rather than replace Git's client and protocol, OpenAI has changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it's being streamed to immutable blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. A metadata transaction records the reference version (containing the latest branch tip, the packfile and its dependencies on earlier reference versions) and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently of one another; updates to the same reference still need to be coordinated.

OpenAI refers to this as causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. A reader gets the history needed for the requested revision, but fetching a number of branches won't provide a repository-wide snapshot. Two clients can see different combinations of branch versions during concurrent updates. The trade-off removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes.

Pando also changes how Git decides which objects to transfer. By default, when a client pushes a newly introduced feature branch, the server will advertise only a designated trunk branch as its base. That constrains the dependencies of the resulting packfile, which in turn allows Pando to reuse it for readers who already have that trunk history. Repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some additional bandwidth for the benefit of reusable packs.

Pando’s topic-branch packs depend on advertised trunk history and can repeat objects from earlier pushes (source).

Industry observers note that for fetches, Pando maps the client's existing and requested commits to reference versions and picks out the appropriate stored packs to cover the missing history. Git's packfile-uri capability allows the server to return download links rather than generate a bespoke pack for each client. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves those downloads. OpenAI reports cache-hit rates in excess of 99% and tests in which clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links.

Background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers, resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree. The covers provide better compression and act as a skip-list-like index for fetch planning. Pando keeps packs at every level so that clients with different histories can still be served.

Pando groups successive packs into larger covers to improve compression and fetch planning, retaining packs at every level (source).

The design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, previously covered by InfoQ. Scion replaces Git's underlying model with changesets recording files changed relative to their first parent and content-addressed pointers to compressed file contents; commits, merges, rebases and history queries run server-side. Its clients retrieve missing immutable trees and blobs, rather than negotiate Git packfiles, and use bounded local caches and sparse or virtualised checkouts.

Recent findings suggest that both systems make use of immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation. The way in which they draw the compatibility line is very different, though. Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows and changes the backend coordination and delivery. Scion, on the other hand, assumes an online client and moves the repository operations into a dedicated service. The improvements they report are not directly comparable. OpenAI reports on push latency, whereas Anthropic reports on checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions compared with its previous Git-based setup.

Recent findings suggest that git compatibility did not eliminate migration work. OpenAI initially deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations using legacy APIs, webhooks and repository downloads. It also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs. OpenAI says some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository.

Industry observers note that for the architects, it's a case of two separate decisions: which source control operations go on the server and which of the consistency and transfer guarantees do the workloads actually need. Pando retains the Git workflows but dispenses with the repository-wide snapshot across branches and accepts redundant transfers in order to reduce the amount of coordination and per-fetch computation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

According to recent reports, the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

Industry observers note that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

It has been revealed that at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We strategy to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script releases its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

In a recent development, A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Recent findings suggest that each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS claims nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space highlights comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

According to recent reports, each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reuters reported on November 26, 2026 that Dragos chief research officer HD Moore had identified MiniMax as the previously unnamed Chinese AI developer in a wider investigation of nearly two million seeded AI prompts. Researchers found private web links being opened later, including when people requested no storage or retention.

Reuters stated the public attribution and the Moscow-region findings were being reported for the first time. The evidence concerns particular URL fetches and later attempts to retrieve code; it does not establish that every prompt or model response sent to MiniMax was disclosed.

The November 19, 2026 research post described the method: prompts carried unique URLs and canary credentials, test secrets with no legitimate use, so later connections to controlled systems would reveal that someone had seen the original request. The testing ran from July through November 2026. For the then-unnamed lab, systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of prompts sent to its models between July and October 2026. The same happened to roughly two-thirds of requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention (ZDR), a setting intended to prevent storage of prompts and responses; fetches typically arrived two or three days later.

Moore told Reuters that links sent through different providers were repeatedly opened from a Singapore internet connection. The pattern appeared when requests were forwarded to MiniMax’s cloud, not when other companies independently ran its models. For customers, that makes the hosting and forwarding path as consequential as the model they selected.

It has been revealed that one incident involving a link sent to MiniMax extended beyond automated fetching. The link appeared in a channel on Feishu, ByteDance’s workplace messaging platform, 24 days after the original prompt and was opened within two minutes on three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. Because Dragos had disclosed only the link’s first eight characters to the provider, the researchers inferred that whoever shared it had access to a stored copy of the full prompt.

Researchers later observed attempts to clone private software repositories referenced in MiniMax requests. Reuters reported that the activity appeared after URL scraping seemed to stop on October 22, 2026; who initiated it and whether any code was obtained remain unclear. Researchers also detected unusual internet activity from the Moscow region involving links submitted to MiniMax, but the evidence did not establish that those links were opened from Russia.

MiniMax remarked in a November 24, 2026 statement that its internal security system extracted URLs and IP addresses from forwarded web traffic into security logs for checks against threat intelligence. Automated security programs and agents subsequently probed some logged URLs. The monitoring was enabled by default on endpoints receiving forwarded requests and included traffic marked ZDR or no data collection.

MiniMax remarked the process recorded extracted addresses rather than full request or response content and did not retain full conversations. Its examination found no evidence that prompts or model responses were disclosed to third parties beyond the URL activity. The company deleted the affected URLs, disabled the mechanism and verified that links were no longer opened on the identified path for current business-to-business traffic. The statement did not address the repository-download attempts or the Feishu incident.

In a recent development, atlas Cloud said in an updated security notice that MiniMax’s explanation matched its finding that links were opened after prompts reached MiniMax, not on Atlas Cloud infrastructure. The company stopped forwarding requests to MiniMax’s official API and warned customers who used MiniMax M3, M2.7 or M3.1 Flash to treat submitted secrets as exposed and revoke affected credentials, tokens or links. Atlas had selected MiniMax’s Singapore data centers to avoid processing customer data in China, a choice that still left information potentially exposed after it reached MiniMax.

In a recent development, novita noted in a privacy notice that a routing-configuration issue sent some MiniMax requests to the official API instead of Novita-hosted infrastructure between May 28, 2026 and November 11, 2026. The affected paths included direct Novita traffic and requests routed through OpenRouter. The investigation found accesses to embedded URLs and hostnames, with no observed use of test markers for Amazon Web Services credentials. Novita advised customers whose requests contained live credentials or other secrets to revoke or rotate them.

OpenRouter noted in a broader November 22, 2026 response that it had off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility and notified potentially affected customers. The platform found no breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself; continuing work included adapting the researchers’ testing and verifying network paths.

MiniMax’s explanation accounts for the automated probes of logged links, while the Feishu sharing and repository-download attempts remain unattributed. The episode makes the full routing path central to AI privacy: no-retention settings did not stop systems along that path from extracting and later using embedded URLs.

Recent findings suggest that LFM3 is our upcoming generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

LFM2 revealed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

The payoff reveals at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two latest in-house encoders:.

Industry observers note that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

It has been revealed that reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

In a recent development, for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

InfoQ Homepage News CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. Fresh research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.

It has been revealed that the report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.

The research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.

The survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

Furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.

It has been revealed that AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates latest risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.

In a recent development, virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.

The survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.

Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

Kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.

In a recent development, the findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain important, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.

For platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly important infrastructure considerations.

The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.

Tech Report: Typed indexes in Zig
