⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.
  • Recent findings suggest that the above examples were not particularly illuminating to me.
  • In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.

Recent findings suggest that the above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call @backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me.

In practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type.

In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming.

Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes:.

We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes.

It has been revealed that its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example.

Our spreadsheet has now several fields: a title, and row and column properties. When iterating over them, we have two kinds of indexes: row indexes and column indexes. Adding typed indexes is attractive to prevent callers from mixing them up.

Recent findings suggest that this enum gives us a way of referencing all the struct fields for which we will construct a typed indexed. If all fields were to be indexed, we would have used std.meta.FieldEnum(Sheet), but our spreadsheet has a title.

Recent findings suggest that this checks at compile time that each Field enum variant name is indeed a field inside Sheet. As we’ll see later, we will have to access Sheet’s fields by name, so it’s good to check the names of Field variants match the names of Sheet fields.

This defines the kind of type indexes we’ll construct: one for row data slices and one for columns data slices. Each indexed field of Sheet has one correct typed index kind. We match them with an exhaustive switch over Field.

Recent findings suggest that we now have all we need to construct the two typed indexes of kinds .row and .col. A generic function returning a type at comptime is how to do it.

Recent findings suggest that the typed index type for row is Sheet.Index(.row), and for colum it is Sheet.Index(.col). Note the title case of the Index function, matching Zig’s convention for types.

Remains to give a way of making use of these types.

Recent findings suggest that this part may look complex if you are not familiar with comptime-enabled generics in Zig, so let’s be precise. This defines a method on Sheet that requires f to be a Field instance known at compile time. This allow to infer at compile time both the type of i and the return type.

According to recent reports, index(kindOf(f)) is just a chain of function calls on a known value. So it is comptime known. And most importantly, the type of i is bound to the one of f at compile time. Given the body of Sheet.kindOf, it’s easy to see that s.at(.row_width, i) will compile only if i has type Index(.row)!

It has been revealed that the return type of Zig function must be comptime known, and it is the case here by using some reflection. @FieldType(Sheet, name) returns the type of the field of Sheet named name (given as a []const u8). @tagName(f) gives just that for the input enum variant. std.meta.Elem returns the element type for a collection type (here a slice). Finally, we return a pointer to allow the caller to mutate, but a value would work just fine for a read-only case.

This gives us a clear usage at call site.

The Sheet.Index(.row) syntax is particularly lovely: a method call feeling like a qualified concrete type.

In a recent development, still, as I hinted earlier, this design it not completely hermetic to bugs. Nothing prevents you from forging a Sheet.Index(.row) from any integer with @fromBackingInt. And opaque types are really just for interaction with C.

Also, any caller can access Sheet fields directly (Zig has no notion of private fields.).

It has been revealed that as for all Zig code, one must follow documented usage (“Direct access is discouraged. Use Sheet.at.”) and make good use of the public methods by proactively inspecting types.

At LINE BIZ CONVERGE 2026 on November 26, 2026, LINE Taiwan mentioned it will pursue a three-part AI agent strategy spanning consumer assistance, brand service and merchant operations, building on more than 3.6 million official accounts to move customer interactions beyond answers toward completed tasks.

Sources indicate that the strategy connects consumer access, brand fulfillment and merchant decision-making. It also places customer-facing agents within a broader product framework covering advertising, commerce and data, tying service interactions to subsequent business activity.

Sources indicate that the planned Consumer Agent would handle everyday needs and connect users to services directly inside chats. Brand Agent, delivered through official accounts, would integrate brand service workflows and complete customer tasks. LINE Biz AI is the Business Agent, intended to combine data insights with operational recommendations and execution support for merchants.

In a recent development, for brands, the upcoming AI agent platform will sit inside OA Plus, the administrative backend for official accounts. Businesses will be able to choose appointment, sales or customer-service agent roles and describe their requirements in natural language, with AI guiding the setup. They will also be able to combine basic and advanced functions according to their operating needs.

LINE Biz AI is designed to use the customer context created by those interactions. Within OA Plus, it would combine appointment records, product or service preferences, official-account interactions and membership information, automatically tag customer profiles and identify audiences. For a nail salon, that could mean recognizing a customer who has not booked recently, recommending a return-visit offer and sending messages when the merchant directs it to do so.

Industry observers note that LINE first detailed the official-account platform in an October 13, 2026 announcement, which said brands could connect their own point-of-sale, customer relationship management, membership, reservation and scheduling systems alongside standard templates. LINE planned to begin brand cooperation and validation at the end of 2026 and targeted a formal launch in the first quarter of 2027.

LINE Biz AI has a separate, staged rollout. It became available on the LINE Biz-Solutions website in November 2026 to provide AI Q&A about products and services. LINE plans to bring it into OA Plus in the first half of 2027 for operational decision and action support, then gradually integrate AI capabilities across products in the second half of 2027 so it can assist across services.

In a recent development, the surrounding products are intended to connect agent interactions to transactions. The Chat Ad format in LINE’s LAP advertising system lets a consumer enter a brand conversation after clicking an ad and ask about a product or service before deciding whether to add the official account as a friend. A separate Cross Buy and LINE Gift test uses previous purchasing and gifting behavior to anticipate future gifting demand, generate ads from LINE Gift product assets and direct consumers back to LINE Gift to complete a purchase.

In a recent development, physical stores provide another entry point. With LINE Touch, a shopper can tap a phone to open a brand’s LINE MINI App, collect coupons and redeem them in-store without downloading a separate app. LINE reports that a FamilyMart trial combining the two products reached a maximum coupon redemption rate of 91%.

Industry observers note that for campaign planning, LINE Data Hub is designed to show audience profiles before ads run and use campaign results afterward to inform subsequent prepares. AI Persona uses semantic analysis across LINE cross-service behavior labels, official-account friend data and user research, allowing brands to explore audience characteristics in natural language and receive suggestions for messaging and ad creative. LINE also plans partnerships under its DMP Alliance data program with Invoice Monster operator Chun Shu Technology, ECPay DATA and uTagGo to add spending, payment, ecommerce and mobility data sources.

Industry observers note that together, those products describe an operating loop in which an ad starts a conversation, an agent completes a service task and the resulting customer information informs the next action. With the main brand and merchant capabilities scheduled in stages through 2027, the practical test is whether those releases form a shared operating loop across OA Plus and LINE’s commerce and data tools, rather than a set of isolated chat features.

📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that language models can do a lot.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • Industry observers note that in our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they mentioned (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

Industry observers note that in our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's latest speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

Sources indicate that it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Recent findings suggest that parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

In a recent development, qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

Industry observers note that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Recent findings suggest that each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Recent findings suggest that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Industry observers note that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who noted what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

Recent findings suggest that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Sources indicate that parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

According to recent reports, these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Sources indicate that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't upcoming, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

According to recent reports, apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

Sources indicate that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

In a recent development, reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

It has been revealed that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

According to recent reports, language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Industry observers note that each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

Recent findings suggest that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Recent findings suggest that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

It has been revealed that each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WaterSense unveiled on November 26, 2026 that it had raised a combined €5.75 million in pre-seed investment and grants to expand AI-supported water-quality monitoring across Europe, including a strategy to monitor the Oder River continuously from its sources to its mouth.

The pre-seed round was co-led by b2venture and Movens Capital, with participation from vastpoint. The announcement separately identifies €3.5 million from Poland’s National Centre for Research and Development for further sensor development and satellite-data integration. That work is intended to add measurements for ammonium ions, nitrates, orthophosphates, fluorides, lead and E. coli, extending analysis from individual stations to entire water bodies and watercourses.

Recent findings suggest that waterSense is addressing a monitoring gap created by manual sampling: field teams collect water at individual sites and send it to laboratories, producing accurate results that can arrive days later and describe only past conditions. Its model replaces those isolated readings with continuously operating autonomous stations connected to a cloud analytics platform, giving utilities, industrial operators and public authorities a current view of rivers, lakes and industrial water systems.

The hardware uses hundreds of inexpensive miniature printed sensors, automatically replaced inside the station instead of relying on one expensive sensor that must remain stable through long exposure. WaterSense claims this limits the impact of biofouling, the buildup of aquatic organisms on equipment, and reduces servicing needs. The sensor design originated in founder Filip Budny’s doctoral research at Warsaw University of Technology.

Industry observers note that waterSense’s product description lists more than 25 water-quality parameters measured every ten minutes. The stations use hybrid solar and optional hydro power, supporting continuous operation without cables or external power infrastructure.

Sources indicate that field readings create a growing reference database connected to satellite observations and deep-learning models. WaterSense says the models can forecast water-quality changes up to 72 hours ahead and that AI agents turn the combined data into alerts, operational conclusions and decision support. The operational goal is earlier warning for intake protection and better-informed treatment decisions.

It has been revealed that the ASIR research project, which is developing an autonomous Internet of Things system for water-quality monitoring and threat identification, runs from September 1, 2024 through August 30, 2027. Alongside the station, it includes cloud-based anomaly detection and an interactive national river-pollution risk map for planning measurements and station placement. Warsaw University of Technology leads a consortium whose other members are the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management, MAGLY and NEBUCODE.

Industry observers note that waterSense reports monitoring more than 80 points for over 30 customers in four European countries. Its customers include industrial operators, large water utilities, cities and regional authorities. They receive continuous measurements, alerts, analysis and decision-support tools through a Data-as-a-Service subscription, under which WaterSense supplies the monitoring infrastructure and customers avoid building their own field teams and measurement systems.

Deployments include alpine lakes in Austria and urban water systems in large European cities. In Kitzbühel, Austria, the monitored parameters include water temperature, conductivity, pH, dissolved oxygen and phycocyanin, a pigment that serves as a blue-green algae indicator. The continuous view is intended to help local teams track changes between field visits and plan environmental stewardship and tourism activities.

It has been revealed that the upcoming capital is intended to move WaterSense beyond individual installations toward a denser monitoring network across European rivers, lakes and water systems. WaterSense states each deployment adds to a geographically varied reference dataset and strengthens its predictive analytics. The Oder project would extend continuous observation and decision support from selected locations to the full length of the river.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement cites the 2022 ecological crisis along hundreds of kilometres of the Oder, which affected water utilities and river-dependent businesses, as an example of decisions being made with information that arrives too late. The planned river-wide deployment gives the tech giant’s network model a concrete test: consistent field measurements and useful forecasts would need to support decisions across connected stretches of water, where pollution can affect consumers far beyond an individual monitoring point.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 Aims to Make Robots Safer, More Dexterous, and Faster Learners.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a vision-language-action (VLA) model designed to improve robots' dexterity, reliability, and learning speed, while enabling safer operation in unstructured real-world environments.

According to DeepMind's vice president and head of robotics Carolina Parada, the model "marks a leap forward in three key areas": dexterity, reliability, and safety. She says its performance has been evaluated across more than 200 tasks, with reported improvements of 30% to 100% in success rates and 20% to 30% in task completion compared with prior versions. Demonstrated capabilities include serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting liquids.

These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse.

The model is designed to work natively with different types of robots, including humanoid platforms such as Apptronik's Apollo 2 and tabletop pick & place systems such as Franka Duo platform.

Sources indicate that parada highlights the industrial trials conducted with Mercedes Benz, in which Apollo 2 humanoid robots were deployed on an existing industrial line, achieving a 96% success rate in tasks involving automotive kitting and sorting mixed metal brackets. In the trial, the Gemini Robotics ER embodied reasoning model enabled the robot to keep track of the workflow over multiple steps and adapt to changeing conditions, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled the robot's hands and arms.

Another key aspect highlighted by Parada is Gemini Robotics 2.5's safety features, which include using reasoning guidance to identify and manage physical hazards:.

Much like safety classifiers add a protective layer around Gemini’s responses, this guidance allows the robot to navigate complex environments securely. In our evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%.

DeepMind also open-sourced the latest safety benchmark ASIMOV-jailbreak, containing hundreds of unsafe prompts across dozens of scenes.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, GEICO director of software Sean P. observed that "the combination of simulation, learning from mistakes, and real-world testing is what will make robots more capable and reliable in everyday tasks".

LightSpeed founder and CEO Biju Kulathakal emphasized that 96% accuracy may not be enough in real contexts involving humans:.

It has been revealed that pausing when a person gets close is what gets robots out from behind the fence. And on a real line, customers live in the 4%. Learning from its own mistakes is how that closes.

Level principal engineer Ariel Franco Ferreira expressed his view that.

Releasing an open benchmark for jailbreaks on a VLA model is the part I find most interesting, because a prompt injection that ends in a physical action is a very different failure from a bad chat answer.

He also raised the question of how to handle situations "when the robot refuses the unsafe step but leaves the task half done in a risky state".

As a final note, Gemini Robotics 2.5's development was accelerated using Gemini 4 Argon as a simulation engine, leveraging its robotics research capabilities to generate simulated environments.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Breaking: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • It has been revealed that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • In a recent development, mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

It has been revealed that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super crucial for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

According to recent reports, mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

Sources indicate that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

It has been revealed that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

According to recent reports, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing indicated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ROBOTERA disclosed in a November 26, 2026 announcement that 45 of its humanoid robots are being tested for parcel induction at China Post’s Hangzhou Postal District Center.

China Post’s Hangzhou center officially launched the testing program in April 2026. ROBOTERA describes it as the largest deployment of robots for testing in comparable postal operations nationwide.

Parcel induction here covers the handling work that moves packages onto induction platforms within a sorting operation. The robots can independently pick parcels, reorient them, identify and reject irregularly shaped parcels, place parcels onto those platforms, and handle operational exceptions.

Sources indicate that that is a broader assignment than a single pick-and-place motion. It combines object recognition, physical manipulation and accept-or-reject decisions with responses to exceptions, giving the fleet several functions within one induction workflow. The testing therefore examines whether humanoids can handle varied parcels and disruptions at a postal facility, rather than only repeat a fixed movement.

ROBOTERA reports that multiple rounds of iterative optimization raised induction efficiency from 500–600 parcels per hour during initial testing to approximately 1,200 parcels per hour during specific testing periods, with operational accuracy above 90% and improvements in motion smoothness, recognition accuracy and handling precision.

In a recent development, those figures describe different aspects of the work: throughput measures speed, while accuracy and handling precision bear on whether parcels are processed correctly. The higher rate applies to particular testing periods, so it represents performance reached during those tests rather than a sustained fleet-wide production average.

It has been revealed that the Hangzhou disclosure follows a separate Guangdong rollout announced on November 17, 2026, which covered 11 postal hubs in eight cities. That project began with a pilot at the Guangzhou Postal District Center in March 2026. ROBOTERA reported an average induction rate above 1,500 parcels per hour there, comparable to the performance of experienced human workers. The rates have different measurement bases: Guangdong’s was an average, while Hangzhou’s higher result came during specific testing periods. The earlier project also spanned a provincial network, whereas Hangzhou concentrates the disclosed fleet at one facility.

China Post’s Hangzhou branch said it plans to accelerate adoption of automated equipment, including intelligent sorting and security-inspection systems, across more operational scenarios to improve postal-delivery quality and efficiency. That initiative would extend automation beyond the induction work covered by the current robot tests.

Industry observers note that hangzhou now provides a concentrated counterpart to the distributed Guangdong project: a single facility where fleet size, multi-step handling and test performance can be assessed together. The branch’s planned expansion into sorting and security inspection broadens the stakes, leaving the operational question of whether the induction results can be maintained as automation covers more of the facility’s workflow.

GigaChat 4 Debuts With 1M-Token Context and Two Model Sizes

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the GigaChat Team revealed GigaChat 4 on November 26, 2026, releasing 708B- and 37B-parameter mixture-of-experts models with native one-million-token context windows.
  • The flagship 708B-A41B uses approximately 41B active parameters per token, compared with roughly 3.8B for the compact 37B-A4B.
  • Both models use a 3:1 mix of Gated DeltaNet layers and multi-head latent attention layers enhanced with DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the GigaChat Team revealed GigaChat 4 on November 26, 2026, releasing 708B- and 37B-parameter mixture-of-experts models with native one-million-token context windows. Both activate only a subset of their parameters per token, support tool calling and multi-step agent tasks, and allow Instant or Reasoning responses to be selected per request within one checkpoint.

The flagship 708B-A41B uses approximately 41B active parameters per token, compared with roughly 3.8B for the compact 37B-A4B. Both were trained on sequences extending to the full context length for work with long documents, collections of sources and large codebases. This arrangement replaces GigaChat 3.5’s separate instant and reasoning checkpoints.

Both models use a 3:1 mix of Gated DeltaNet layers and multi-head latent attention layers enhanced with DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). Gated DeltaNet maintains a fixed-size recurrent state, while DSA selects up to 2,048 earlier positions for each query rather than computing attention over the entire sequence. The companion technical report says indexer and selection overhead can outweigh the attention savings at short contexts or small decode batches.

Recent findings suggest that the flagship has 64 decoder layers and 256 routed experts, selecting eight per token together with one shared expert. The compact model has 32 layers and 192 routed experts, using the same combination of eight routed experts and one shared expert.

For the 708B model, context extension progressed from 32K to 128K tokens before indexer training and joint optimization at the native length. After supervised fine-tuning, specialist models underwent reinforcement learning in mathematics, coding, tool use and multi-turn agent workflows. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation then consolidated their capabilities into one model offering both response modes.

Recent findings suggest that under the team’s evaluation protocol, the 708B model scored 71.26% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 in Reasoning mode and 60.47% in Instant mode, versus 30.30% and 12.94% respectively for GigaChat 3.5. Its reported Reasoning results also include 80.89% on SWE-bench Verified and 79.55% on BFCL v4, although GLM-5.3 is listed higher at 86.67% on SWE-bench Verified.

The compact model’s reported Reasoning results include 85.00% on LiveCodeBench v6, 70.80% on SWE-bench Verified and 72.00% on BFCL. For the flagship, evaluation combined public runners and scoring code with the team’s own implementations, including seven-hour timeouts for specified agentic benchmarks.

The team’s demonstrations emphasize tasks that chain artifacts and tools: the flagship modified a Mario cartridge’s palette in its binary file and ran the game on a Mac M4, produced an STL vase for 3D printing, and used MCP access to the Cadenza music workstation to compose a track before building an accompanying visualization site.

The flagship model card lists FP8, BF16 and GGUF instruction-tuned variants, along with base and intermediate checkpoints, and releases its instruction-tuned checkpoint under the MIT License. The compact model card lists the same variant categories but uses the Noncommercial License for Individuals 1.0. The detailed technical report currently covers the 708B model; a dedicated report for the 37B model is planned for later.

According to recent reports, both cards document SGLang and vLLM serving, per-request mode selection and OpenAI-compatible tool calling. They recommend Pi for agentic tasks, with Codex CLI and DeepSeek Harness as alternatives for interactive terminal work.

The flagship’s documented FP8 configuration uses two nodes with eight H100 80 GB GPUs each. The compact model’s example uses one H100 80 GB GPU, with approximately 40 GB required for its weights before attention caches, recurrent states and activations.

Sources indicate that gigaChat 4 makes deployment terms part of the model choice alongside benchmark scores: the flagship combines MIT licensing with a two-node example, while the compact model offers a single-GPU path under noncommercial terms. For prospective people, the compact checkpoint’s usage restrictions are therefore as consequential as its lower hardware requirement.

Breaking: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • It has been revealed that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

It has been revealed that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

According to recent reports, participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Recent findings suggest that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

According to recent reports, the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

It has been revealed that the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Fresh public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

It has been revealed that when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an vital part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

It has been revealed that publicly available genomic data has proved vital in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support latest research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Recent findings suggest that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an key first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

In a recent development, to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

In a recent development, the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

In a recent development, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

According to recent reports, beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Sources indicate that teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be unveiled through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or manufacturer building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

Tech Report: Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance.
  • Nov 26, 2026 10 min read.
  • Microsoft Ignite 2026, held in San Francisco and online from November 17 to 20, centered on running AI agents in production, with Microsoft positioning Copilot as the operating system for work and extending agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance.

Nov 26, 2026 10 min read.

Microsoft Ignite 2026, held in San Francisco and online from November 17 to 20, centered on running AI agents in production, with Microsoft positioning Copilot as the operating system for work and extending agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender.

Sources indicate that CEO Satya Nadella opened the keynote by acknowledging the November 12 Microsoft 365 outage, then positioned Copilot as the operating system for work, combining chat, coding, and autonomous agents in one experience. In his edited keynote remarks, Nadella argued that customers must be able to examine and independently verify what AI does, declared an AI Transparency Initiative aligned with NIST's Agent Standards Initiative, and rejected setups where models audit other models:.

These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable.

The Book of News groups the announcements by product area, and many of them ship as previews rather than in general availability.

Sources indicate that azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines are now generally available, a year after InfoQ reported on Microsoft introducing the chip at Ignite 2025 and two and a half years after the preview of Cobalt 100 VMs. According to the Azure announcement, the processor combines 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores on TSMC's 3nm process, and the VMs run in 14 regions today, with 23 planned by the end of 2026. Microsoft claims up to 50% better CPU performance than Cobalt 100, plus up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS through Azure Boost. Customers can run cores at a fixed 3.2 GHz in Deterministic Mode or let them boost up to 3.6 GHz in Opportunistic Mode, and the lineup adds Mpsv4 VMs for high-memory workloads and storage-optimized Lpsv5 VMs. Amadeus reported more than 30% higher flight-search throughput than on Cobalt 100, and OpenAI's Vadim Filanovsky described a similar result:.

We saw higher throughput and lower latency on Cobalt 200.

Confidential computing gains three previews: multi-GPU confidential computing on VR72 for models larger than a single GPU, Azure Confidential Enclaves with AKS Kata CoCo containers, and Azure Confidential Clean Room for multiparty analytics without exposing raw data.

Customers can now deploy Foundry open-weight models and agents to their own AKS clusters. At the same time, an Agent Sandbox extension provides VM-level isolation for agent-written code, and Agent Grid applies central policy to agent, model, tool, and service interactions. Flex nodes extend AKS clusters to servers outside Azure. According to the AKS team's Ignite post, managed GPU node pools, which handle GPU drivers, device plugins, and Azure Monitor metrics, are generally available, with NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 support and mixed multi-instance GPU in preview. Confidential VM node pools on Azure Container Linux are also generally available on both Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP VM sizes.

On the operations side, Azure Monitor health models are generally available and build a real-time health graph from telemetry, ranking incidents by business impact. The Azure Copilot deployment agent, also generally available, turns natural-language requirements into deployed workloads, and Azure SRE Agent picks up previews for customer-managed keys, Entra Agent ID integration, cross-agent communication, and multicloud investigations. For migration projects, Azure Catalyst is now generally available, with its agent (formerly the Azure Copilot migration agent) handling discovery, assessment, and planning. Separately, GitHub Copilot modernization adds a preview of BizTalk-to-Logic Apps migration.

Microsoft now pitches Sovereign Private Cloud as a full stack on Azure Local, with VMs and AKS at the base, followed by data services, Foundry Local, GitHub Enterprise Local, and Microsoft 365 Local. Darryl van der Peijl, a Microsoft MVP for Azure Local, Hyper-V, and Azure Arc, listed what shipped in his Azure Local Insider newsletter: Foundry Local on Azure Local and GitHub Enterprise Local are generally available, while a Sovereign control panel, Blob Storage and DocumentDB on Azure Local, multi-tenancy, and rehoming are in preview. The control panel assesses data residency, encryption, network exposure, and business continuity for Azure resources without enforcing any controls, and during the preview it runs in European regions only, with the service hosted in Sweden.

Van der Peijl singled out rehoming, which moves an Azure Local instance from Azure management to local management while VMs, AKS clusters, and data stay in place:.

Until now, going from connected to disconnected meant a migration project. Microsoft showed a script that does the rehoming in one run.

It has been revealed that azure Local also runs on arm64 for the first time, in public preview on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Development Kit, which hosts containers on bare metal without a hypervisor. Windows Server 2028 entered preview through the Windows Server Insider Program, bringing a hardened Server Core, post-quantum cryptography, native NVMe enabled by default, NVMe over Fabrics, and boot from ReFS. According to van der Peijl, Microsoft added inference as a newly introduced pillar for the release, calling on-premises inference servers token factories, and is moving network drivers from kernel mode to user mode as part of its Windows resiliency work. Windows Admin Center vMode is now generally available at no extra cost and manages up to 1,000 Hyper-V hosts and 25,000 VMs, which Microsoft described on stage as "kind of a replacement for SCVMM.".

Foundry's main theme was continuous improvement. Multi-turn evaluation and production insights that group recurring failures and rank fixes are now generally available, while the agent optimizer, human annotation, rubric evaluators, Managed Training, and Programmed Training for custom SFT and reinforcement learning loops on open-weight models are in preview. The optimizer adjusts an agent's instructions, skills, and model choice, with a human approving each change before it ships.

In a separate engineering post, the Microsoft team behind the optimizer described how the loop works. They reported that the reflector, a separate model that reads failing traces and diagnoses why an agent scored poorly, influenced results more than switching the agent's own model, for example between gpt-4o and gpt-4.1-mini. Developers drive the loop from the Azure Developer CLI:.

Writing on DEV Community, Hector Flores advised readers to treat Microsoft's claim that the model router saves up to 65% compared with a frontier model as a ceiling rather than a forecast, and he welcomed the human approval step in the optimizer loop:.

Self-modifying agents with no review gate are an incident waiting to happen.

On the model front, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is generally available in Foundry, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Built on Gemma 4 26B A4B with added image input, it scores 68 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 and runs more than twice as fast as its predecessor, and Copilot uses it to route requests. MAI-Code-2 and MAI-Code-2-Flash are generally available on GitHub, MAI-Image-2.7 is in preview, and the model router now covers the top 50 models in a catalog of more than 11,000. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol became generally available in Foundry, with Global Standard deployments covering 28 regions. On Standard deployments with short context, Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, while Astra costs $8 and $40. Foundry IQ added knowledge graphs and an iterative retrieval model, Microsoft-Retriever-1, both in preview.

Sources indicate that microsoft also made Azure AI Gateway generally available as a standalone product, split out of the API Management AI tier, to govern, route, and monitor access to AI models and MCP tools across providers. It includes 10,000 free requests per gateway per month, with paid billing starting January 1, 2027, across 17 regions.

Microsoft IQ, which Nadella described as an externalization of the context system behind Copilot, is now generally available without a fresh SKU. It exposes Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ context to Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Foundry, and MCP-compatible harnesses, and Web IQ is now available to all Azure customers at a lower price. Business plugins, which package reusable context, skills, and tools with hierarchical inheritance and governance, are available through the Frontier program.

It has been revealed that postgreSQL got most of the attention on the data side. Azure HorizonDB is now generally available as a managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database with built-in vector indexing, and teams can lock it down with Entra ID, private endpoints, and their own encryption keys. Calling models from SQL through AI Functions and AI Pipelines is still in preview. The same holds for Fabric HorizonDB, a serverless variant inside Fabric that provisions in seconds and pauses when nobody uses it, and for a DMS path that moves existing Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers onto HorizonDB.

Teams moving off Oracle can test a fresh Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration in Azure DMS, also in preview. Cosmos DB developers now have a generally available Rust SDK and semantic reranker, and Cosmos DB Shell lets them query from VS Code or the portal with MCP support built in. On Azure Managed Redis, the Redis 8 preview folds JSON, search, time-series, and vector search into a single version. Anyone who wants to develop against Azure SQL Database on a laptop can pull a preview container that needs no Azure subscription.

The Microsoft Copilot SDK 2.0 is generally available, built on a native Rust runtime, supported in six languages, and using the same agent harness Microsoft and GitHub run internally. The GitHub Copilot app now takes Azure DevOps repositories from clone to merge and runs tests in a real, signed-in browser. Copilot code review adds local reviews in the CLI and app, secret detection, adaptive review effort, and cross-repository context. Copilot Code, a natural-language app builder with cloud and local sandboxes, is in the Frontier program, with general availability planned for December and a macOS local sandbox still to come.

Sources indicate that the Copilot app now brings Chat, Cowork, Code, and Autopilot into one experience, and Office in Copilot puts Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside it as a generally available feature. Autopilot, a long-running personal agent with its own identity, memory, and tool access, is rolling out to Frontier customers. Salesforce in Copilot entered preview with more than 38 prebuilt sales skills, and zero-copy data federation between Salesforce Data 360 and Fabric OneLake is generally available. For spend control, Agent 365 FinOps previews cost visibility, policies, alerts, and Fabric-based chargeback.

Cost tracking also featured in practitioner reactions. In his newsletter, Microsoft principal AI apps architect Anurag Karuparti wrote that tokenomics is among the top challenges his customers raise, and he proposed a different unit for agent ROI:.

Recent findings suggest that the metric that matters isn't just tokens consumed. It's cost per successful business outcome. That's how I think enterprises should start measuring agent ROI.

Writing for business leaders, Aaron Reich, CTO of the Accenture and Microsoft joint venture Avanade, built his Ignite analysis around trust rather than speed:.

Sources indicate that speed isn't the bottleneck anymore, trust is. As AI drives the cost of knowledge toward zero with apps being easier to build, agents doing more work, and abundant intelligence, the scarce things are hard and need more attention: institutional knowledge, judgment, accountability and trust.

At the Microsoft Hub, where he spent the week answering customer questions, Microsoft MVP Muhammad Atif noticed a change in what customers wanted to know:.

It has been revealed that how do we actually put this into production? How do we scale AI and agents across the organisation? How do we govern and secure them? How do we control the cost as adoption grows?

Entra now assigns Agent IDs automatically to discovered local agents, starting with GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, and previews an MCP Firewall that controls access to MCP servers, tools, prompts, and transports. The Microsoft MCP Server for Enterprise, which gives agents permission-controlled access to Entra data, is generally available. Defender's runtime protection for local AI agents on Windows is generally available to Defender for Endpoint P2 customers, while Intune previews local agent governance that marks devices with unapproved agents as noncompliant. Agent 365 now has a generally available tools registry that lists the plugins, skills, MCP servers, and connectors agents use; MCP governance is in preview through Azure AI Gateway and LiteLLM; and Dynamic Agent Risk combines runtime, posture, and blast-radius signals into risk levels for each agent. Microsoft Perception, formerly Project Perception, is now generally available, with its Triage Agent covering about 80% of alerts in a typical Defender queue.

(Source: Microsoft Tech Community, Agent 365 blog).

In her Ignite recap, cloud and identity consultant Shannon Kuehn warned against handling agents as ordinary applications:.

Treat agents like apps and you'll spend 2027 cleaning up after them.

The complete list of announcements is available in the Microsoft Ignite 2026 Book of News, and Microsoft has made keynote and breakout session recordings available on demand on the Ignite website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SIMMTECH’s board approved two KRW 150 billion private perpetual bond issues on November 26, 2026 to expand production of AI-oriented SOCAMM module substrates and high-layer MSAP substrates, according to convertible-bond and bond-with-warrants decisions filed through South Korea’s DART corporate-disclosure system.

Sources indicate that the Series 11 securities are unsecured private perpetual convertible bonds; Series 12 comprises unsecured, non-detachable private perpetual bonds with warrants. Each filing designates the full amount as facility funds for the two substrate categories from December 2026 through December 2027, with no allocation to working capital or debt repayment. Subscriptions occurred on the approval date, while cash payment is scheduled for December 4, 2026, so the disclosures cover an approved financing before the proceeds are received.

SIMMTECH approved KRW 274.2 billion in an August 25, 2026 capacity-investment decision for a dedicated AI-oriented SOCAMM module-substrate factory and additional high-layer MSAP substrate capacity through December 31, 2027. That decision cited increasing demand for both product categories and identified internal resources or external financing, excluding a rights offering, as the funding sources. The November approvals supply a defined external financing structure for the same two substrate categories, rather than marking a change in product direction.

Both series carry an initial 3% coupon and maturity yield and mature on December 4, 2056. Full conversion or warrant exercise for either series would produce 1,409,906 common shares at KRW 106,390 per share, equivalent to 3.54% of SIMMTECH’s existing shares for that series. Conversion and exercise rights open on December 4, 2027 and run through November 4, 2056.

Sources indicate that the Series 11 capital-securities terms and corresponding Series 12 terms allow SIMMTECH to defer interest at its discretion, with unpaid amounts accumulating additional interest. The company can also extend maturity on the same issuance conditions, while holders have no right to demand early redemption.

According to recent reports, from December 4, 2029, the coupon and maturity yield increase by four percentage points, followed by annual one-percentage-point increases capped at 19%. SIMMTECH may redeem either series quarterly beginning on that date, giving it a scheduled route to retire the securities as their cost rises.

SIMMTECH reported preliminary third-quarter 2026 results showing consolidated revenue of KRW 535.9 billion, up 43.7% from a year earlier, and operating profit of KRW 101.8 billion, up 721.6%. The figures are unaudited and subject to change during accounting review. The resulting operating margin is roughly 19%, calculated from the reported revenue and operating profit.

It has been revealed that the disclosures frame the expansion’s financing trade-off: SIMMTECH has arranged long-dated capital for AI-substrate capacity, investors hold routes into common shares, and the manufacturer faces escalating coupons on securities left outstanding. The balance among conversion, warrant exercise and redemption after the step-ups begin will shape whether the larger effect comes through dilution or interest expense.

It has been revealed that with an analytical and engineering-driven perspective, Theo examines how advances in GPUs, custom silicon, memory architectures, and distributed systems enable new generations of AI models. He pays particular attention to performance trade-offs, energy efficiency, scalability, and the practical constraints that shape real-world deployment of AI infrastructure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding upcoming expertise on a single endpoint.

Recent findings suggest that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this patch. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the upcoming multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.
